claim: Circuits along the ascending somatosensory pathway through mouse hand/forelimb S1 and M1 were recently described in detail by Yamawaki et al., 2021.
source: Circuits along the ascending somatosensory pathway through mouse hand/forelimb S1 and M1 were recently described in detail (Yamawaki et al., 2021).

source: Brief (5 ms) optogenetic photostimulation of the hand generated short (~25 ms) barrages of activity first in S1 (onset latency 15 ms) then M1 (10 ms later).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The estimated propagation speed was 20-fold faster from hand to S1 than from S1 to M1.
source: The estimated propagation speed was 20-fold faster from hand to S1 than from S1 to M1.
evidence: The claim is supported by calculations based on experimental measurements of latencies and distances.

claim: Amplitudes in M1 were strongly attenuated compared to S1.
source: Amplitudes in M1 were strongly attenuated.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data comparing response amplitudes in S1 and M1.

claim: Responses were typically triphasic, with suppression and rebound following the initial peak.
source: Responses were typically triphasic, with suppression and rebound following the initial peak.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing the temporal pattern of responses.

claim: Evoked activity in M1 was biased to upper layers, consistent with corticocortical connectivity.
source: while that in M1 was biased to upper layers, consistent with corticocortical connectivity.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data on laminar profiles and inference based on known corticocortical connectivity patterns.

claim: Parvalbumin (PV) inhibitory interneurons were involved in each phase of the response.
source: Parvalbumin (PV) inhibitory interneurons were involved in each phase
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from opto-tagging experiments.

claim: PV inhibitory interneurons accounted for three quarters of the initial spikes generated in S1.
source: accounting for three quarters of the initial spikes generated in S1

claim: Selective photostimulation of PV interneurons sufficed to evoke suppression and rebound in both S1 and M1.
source: and their selective photostimulation sufficed to evoke suppression and rebound in both S1 and M1.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from selective PV photostimulation experiments.

claim: Partial silencing of S1 by PV activation during hand stimulation reduced the M1 sensory responses.
source: Partial silencing of S1 by PV activation during hand stimulation reduced the M1 sensory responses.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from combined hand and S1 PV stimulation experiments.

claim: Somatosensory signals reach primary motor cortex.
source: Somatosensory signals reach primary motor cortex (Goldring et al., 1970; Strick and Preston, 1982; Swadlow, 1994; Naito et al., 2002; Ferezou et al., 2007; Hatsopoulos and Suminski, 2011; Mao et al., 2011; Murray and Keller, 2011; Alonso et al., 2023; Reddy et al., 2024).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Signals from mechanoreceptor afferents ascend primarily via lemniscal pathways and somatosensory thalamus to arrive in primary somatosensory cortex (S1).
source: To do so, signals from mechanoreceptor afferents ascend primarily via lemniscal pathways and somatosensory thalamus to arrive in primary somatosensory cortex (S1)
evidence: The claim is based on established scientific knowledge about somatosensory pathways.

claim: S1 sends corticocortical projections to primary motor cortex (M1).
source: which sends corticocortical projections to primary motor cortex (M1).
evidence: The claim is based on established scientific knowledge about corticocortical connectivity.

claim: The thalamus→S1→M1 circuits are well studied in model systems such as the rodent vibrissal pathways.
source: The thalamus→S1→M1 circuits are well studied in model systems such as the rodent vibrissal pathways (Ferezou et al., 2007; Mao et al., 2011; Sreenivasan et al., 2016; Petersen, 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior research on vibrissal pathways.

claim: A salient feature of the hand/forelimb circuits is the transition, on reaching S1 cortex, from a 'streamlined' organization of the ascending subcortical circuits via thalamus to a 'densely polysynaptic' organization of the local and interareal cortical circuits.
source: A salient feature of the hand/forelimb circuits is the transition, on reaching S1 cortex, from a 'streamlined' organization of the ascending subcortical circuits via thalamus to a 'densely polysynaptic' organization of the local and interareal cortical circuits (Yamawaki et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Yamawaki et al., 2021.

claim: Crossing a proprioceptor-specific driver line of mice (PV-Cre) with a channelrhodopsin-2 (ChR2) reporter line (Ai32) yielded expression of ChR2 in peripheral mechanoreceptor afferents, particularly around the palm.
source: Crossing a proprioceptor-specific driver line of mice (PV-Cre) with a channelrhodopsin-2 (ChR2) reporter line (Ai32) yielded expression of ChR2 in peripheral mechanoreceptor afferents, particularly around the palm (Figure 1A, Methods).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data and shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The PV-Cre line fortuitously also labels parvalbumin-type GABAergic neurons in the cortex.
source: We chose this line because it fortuitously also labels parvalbumin-type GABAergic neurons in the cortex
evidence: The claim is based on known properties of the PV-Cre mouse line.

claim: Hand stimulation evoked activity in forelimb M1 but did not evoke movements of the forelimb.
source: Although hand stimulation evoked activity in forelimb M1, it did not evoke movements of the forelimb (Figure 1—video 1; Figure 1—figure supplement 1).

claim: In S1, responses begin ~15 ms after stimulus onset and reach peak amplitude ~6 ms later.
source: In S1, responses begin ~15 ms after stimulus onset and reach peak amplitude ~6 ms later.

source: In M1, responses have a similar temporal profile but with a ~10 ms lag and approximately one-third of the S1 amplitude.

claim: In both areas, responses self-terminate, extinguishing within ~25 ms.
source: In both areas, responses self-terminate, extinguishing within ~25 ms.

source: The fraction of all stimulus-responsive units that showed post-peak suppression was relatively small (22.3% in S1, 8.4% in M1)

source: Rebound activity in S1 was observed in 30.9% of stimulus-responsive units, firing on average at 31.4 Hz

source: while rebound activity in M1 involved 8.1% of stimulus-responsive units firing at 20.2 Hz

claim: In both S1 and M1, responses to the second stimulus fell to approximately half the amplitude of the first during the suppressed interval, returning to normal during the rebound interval and after.

claim: In S1, evoked activity was distributed somewhat broadly across cortical layers, with the strongest activity biased to the middle layers.

source: In both areas, the laminar profile of the rebound responses resembled, and were strongly correlated with, those of the initial peak responses (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).

claim: The proportion of stimulus-responsive units among the PV units (64.0%) was higher than among non-PV units (31.1%).
source: The proportion of stimulus-responsive units among the PV units (64.0%) was also higher than among non-PV units (31.1%) (Figure 6E).

claim: PV units collectively accounted for most of the evoked spikes (76.1%).

source: The initial peak responses arrived with ~5 ms shorter latency for PV than for non-PV units (Figure 6G)

claim: The evoked firing of PV units leads that of non-PV units by several milliseconds, consistent with prior observations of vibrissal S1 cortical responses to whisker deflection.
source: Indeed, the evoked firing of PV units even leads that of non-PV units by several milliseconds, consistent with prior observations of vibrissal S1 cortical responses to whisker deflection (Yu et al., 2016).

claim: The selective activation of PV units in S1 cortex can generate a pattern of suppression and rebound closely resembling that observed with hand stimulation.

source: When S1 was partially silenced during hand stimulation, responses in S1 fell to 69.7% of control levels overall

source: These results thus indicate that the responsiveness of M1 to peripheral stimulation of the hand depends at least in part on propagation of sensory-evoked activity via S1.

claim: The hand-to-S1 distance was estimated as 44.3 ± 1.1 mm.
source: The hand-to-S1 distance was estimated as 44.3 ± 1.1 mm

source: and the hand-to-S1 propagation speed was accordingly 3.0 ± 0.1 m/s based on onset latencies

claim: In humans the hand-to-S1 latency is ~20 ms.
source: Interestingly, in humans the hand-to-S1 latency is similarly short, ~20 ms, with correspondingly much higher conduction velocities for the ascending pathways (Desmedt and Cheron, 1980).

source: This speed is comparable to the conduction velocity of thin unmyelinated cortical axons, estimated to be ~0.2 m/s (Raastad and Shepherd, 2003)

source: and to interareal propagation speeds in other corticocortical circuits in mouse cortex, estimated to be approximately 0.3 m/s (Li et al., 2018).

source: Response profiles resemble the 'packet'-like activity patterns previously described in diverse circuits, which have been proposed as fundamental units of information processing in neural systems (Luczak et al., 2015).

claim: Response profiles closely resemble those of optogenetically evoked activity patterns observed in higher-order corticocortical pathways.
source: They also closely resemble those of optogenetically evoked activity patterns observed in higher-order corticocortical pathways (Li et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is based on comparison to prior research cited.

source: For example, cellular-level mechanisms such as spike frequency adaptation rapidly attenuate firing of mouse S1 and M1 neurons (Hattox and Nelson, 2007; Suter et al., 2013).

claim: Prior studies indicate similarly strong, short-latency recruitment of fast-spiking neurons in hand/forelimb M1.

claim: Rebound is an inherent property of the cortex, elicitable not only by peripheral sensory input but also intracortically by PV activation or electrical stimulation.

claim: The optogenetic method for peripheral stimulation used here closely mimics basic features of natural somatosensory stimulation.

claim: Electrical stimulation non-specifically activates somatosensory afferents, including pain fibers.

source: For example, somatosensory thalamus projects not only to S1 but also S2, which projects to M1 (Suter and Shepherd, 2015).
